did_you_know.text: Ezekiel is commanded to prophesy against Israel’s prophets who “prophesy from their own hearts”—that is, they present their words as prophecy even though they have not been commissioned by the LORD.
The false prophets are compared to foxes among the ruins—foxes wandering through devastated places. This image criticizes those who operate amid a ruined reality without repairing it.

The LORD accuses the prophets of not going up to the breaches or building a wall around the house of Israel. Their role, as described here, was to warn and protect the people in a time of danger, but they failed to do so.

The punishment of the false prophets is described in three ways: they will not belong to the council of the LORD’s people, they will not be included in the record of the house of Israel, and they will not enter the land of Israel. Thus, both their influence and their public and national standing are taken away.

The false prophets say, “Peace,” when there is no peace, and they are compared to people who plaster over a weak wall with poor-quality plaster. The wall and plaster symbolize an outward sense of security that rests on no real foundation.

The poor-quality plaster will not withstand torrential rain, hailstones, and storm winds. Through this image of violent natural forces, the chapter emphasizes that reality will expose the weakness of this false security.

In the second half of the chapter, Ezekiel addresses women who prophesy from their own hearts and use coverings and charms to hunt down souls. Here too, the prophecy condemns the use of religious or magical means to influence and deceive people.

The women are accused of profaning the LORD’s name “for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread”—the small payment mentioned in the verse—and of killing people who should not have died and keeping alive people who should not have lived.

The criticism is not only about the falsehood itself: the false prophetesses discouraged the righteous, even though the LORD had not discouraged them, while strengthening the hands of the wicked so that they would not turn from their evil ways.

The chapter concludes by promising the end of the false visions and magic and the rescue of the people of Israel from the women’s power. In this way, the chapter returns to its central purpose: distinguishing the word of the LORD from deceptive human messages.
